faq.q: What should I know before starting?
faq.a: The basics: entering data, writing simple formulas, SUM, AVERAGE, IF and absolute references. If you are new to Excel, take Basic Microsoft Excel first.

faq.q: Do I need Microsoft Excel installed?
faq.a: No. The labs run in your browser with a spreadsheet that behaves like Excel for everything taught here. The skills carry straight over to Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice. A few desktop features such as PivotTables, conditional formatting and Goal Seek are explained and you build the same results with formulas.
About fourteen hours, in short sessions. Each module takes around two to two and a half hours.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your GrowQR profile.

activities.title: Tiered commission with IFS
activities.objective: Replace a tangle of nested IFs with one readable IFS formula.
activities.scenario: A sales team earns commission by band: 10% on sales of 100,000 or more, 7% from 60,000, 5% from 30,000 and 2% below that. Work out each person's rate and commission.
steps: In C2 write an IFS that tests the largest band first and ends with TRUE and the lowest rate.
Write the same kind of formula in C3 to C6, each pointing at its own sales cell.
In D2 multiply the sales by the rate, then do the same for D3 to D6.
In D7 add the five commissions.

checks.label: C2 gives Asha's rate (10%)
checks.explain: IFS tests each condition in order and returns the answer for the first one that is true. Put the biggest band first.

checks.label: C3 gives Bilal's rate (7%)
checks.explain: 75,000 fails the 100,000 test, then passes the 60,000 test.

checks.label: C4 gives Chitra's rate (5%)
checks.explain: 40,000 is below 60,000 but at least 30,000.

checks.label: C6 gives Esha's rate (2%)
checks.hint: The last test is TRUE, which catches everything below 30,000.
checks.explain: A final TRUE condition is the catch-all, like ELSE in other tools.

checks.label: D2 is Asha's commission
checks.explain: Commission is sales times rate.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: If a cell shows #N/A, check that the last IFS test is TRUE.
checks.explain: IFS returns #N/A when none of its tests is true.

activities.title: A price grid with mixed references
activities.objective: Write one formula with mixed references that fills a whole grid correctly.
activities.scenario: Unit prices run down column A and order sizes run across row 1. Every cell in the grid is price times size. One formula, written once and copied, should do it.
steps: In B2 write =$A2*B$1: the dollar sign locks column A for the price and row 1 for the size.
Write the same pattern in C2 and D2, moving only the column letter of the size.
Fill B3:D4 the same way, changing only the row number of the price.

checks.label: B2 is 5 times 10 with mixed references
checks.explain: $A2 keeps the price column fixed; B$1 keeps the size row fixed. That is what lets one formula be copied across and down.

spec.patternMsg: Lock the price column and the size row: =$A2*B$1.

checks.label: C2 is 5 times 20
checks.explain: Copying right moves B to C in the size reference, but the price still comes from column A.

spec.patternMsg: Use $A2 for the price and C$1 for the size.

checks.label: C3 is 8 times 20
checks.explain: Copying down moves 2 to 3 in the price reference, but the size still comes from row 1.

spec.patternMsg: Use $A3 for the price and C$1 for the size.

checks.label: D4 is 12 times 50
checks.explain: The corner of the grid uses the last price and the last size.

spec.patternMsg: Use $A4 for the price and D$1 for the size.

checks.label: B4 is 12 times 10
checks.explain: Each cell in the grid has its own price and its own size.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: A #VALUE! usually means a reference points at a heading.
checks.explain: Errors tell you a reference points somewhere unexpected.

activities.title: Handle errors gracefully
activities.objective: Use IFERROR so one bad row does not break a report.
activities.scenario: Cost per unit is the cost divided by the units. One item has zero units, which would show #DIV/0!. Show "n/a" for it instead, then count the items that do have a cost per unit.
steps: In D2 divide the cost by the units, wrapped in IFERROR with "n/a" as the fallback.
Fill D3 to D5 the same way.
In D7 count how many cost-per-unit values are numbers.

checks.label: D2 is 10
checks.explain: IFERROR runs the first formula and, only if it fails, shows the fallback instead.

checks.label: D3 shows n/a for the book
checks.hint: Same formula; the division by zero is caught.
checks.explain: Catching an expected error keeps a report readable.

checks.label: D4 is 200
checks.explain: 800 divided by 4 is 200.

checks.label: D5 is 5
checks.explain: 30 divided by 6 is 5.

checks.label: D7 counts three numbers
checks.explain: COUNT skips the text "n/a", so it counts only the real prices.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.explain: A clean sheet has no raw error codes.

activities.title: Price an order with VLOOKUP
activities.objective: Look up an item and its price from a table by product code, with the table locked in place.
activities.scenario: An order lists product codes and quantities. The price list is in G1:I5. Fill in the item name and price for each line, then the amount and the order total.
steps: In C2 look up the code in A2 in the price list and return the item name (column 2). Lock the table with dollar signs.
In D2 look up the same code and return the price (column 3).
Fill rows 3 and 4 the same way.
In E2 multiply quantity by price, fill E3 and E4, and total them in E5.

checks.label: C2 finds the item for P3 (Bag)
checks.explain: VLOOKUP searches the first column of the table for the code and returns the value from the column you name.

spec.patternMsg: Lock the table with dollar signs: $G$2:$I$5, so it does not slide when copied.

checks.label: D2 finds the price for P3 (800)
checks.explain: Only the column number changes; the key and the table stay the same.

checks.label: D3 finds the price for P1 (12)
checks.explain: The key moves down a row, the locked table does not.

checks.label: D4 finds the price for P4 (30)
checks.explain: The code P4 sits in the last row of the table.

checks.label: E2 is the amount for the bags (1,600)
checks.explain: Amount is quantity times price.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: FALSE as the last value asks for an exact match.
checks.explain: Without FALSE, VLOOKUP assumes a sorted list and can return a wrong row.

activities.title: Discount slabs with an approximate match
activities.objective: Use VLOOKUP with TRUE to find the band a number falls into.
activities.scenario: A shop gives a discount by spend: 0% below 1,000, 5% from 1,000, 10% from 5,000 and 15% from 10,000. The table lists where each band starts, in ascending order.
steps: In C2 look up the spend in B2 in the band table (F2:G5) and return the discount. Use TRUE for an approximate match.
Fill C3 to C5.
In D2 work out what the customer pays: the spend times one minus the discount. Fill D3 to D5.

checks.label: C2 is 0% for 800
checks.explain: An approximate match finds the largest band start that is not above the value.

checks.label: C3 is 5% for 2,500
checks.explain: 2,500 is at least 1,000 but below 5,000.

checks.label: C4 is 10% for exactly 5,000
checks.explain: A value equal to a band start belongs to that band.

checks.label: C5 is 15% for 12,000
checks.explain: 12,000 is above the last band start, so the last band applies.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: The band table must start at 0 so that small spends still match.
checks.explain: If the first band started at 1,000, a spend of 800 would give #N/A.

activities.title: A two-way lookup with INDEX and MATCH
activities.objective: Find a value by a row heading and a column heading, and find which row holds the biggest number.
activities.scenario: Quarterly sales are in a table with regions down the side and quarters across the top. A manager types a region and a quarter and wants the sales figure, and also asks which region did best in Q4.
steps: In H3 return the sales for the region in H1 and the quarter in H2: INDEX on B2:E5, with MATCH to find the row and MATCH to find the column.
In H5 find the name of the region with the highest Q4 sales: INDEX on the region names, MATCH on the biggest Q4 figure.

checks.label: H3 returns South's Q3 sales (110)
checks.explain: The first MATCH finds the row, the second finds the column, and INDEX returns the cell where they cross.

checks.label: H5 names the best Q4 region (East)
checks.explain: MAX finds the biggest number, MATCH finds its position, INDEX turns the position into a name.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: Use 0 as the last MATCH value for an exact match.
checks.explain: MATCH with 0 looks for an exact match and never guesses.

activities.title: Answer questions with SUMIFS and COUNTIFS
activities.objective: Use several conditions at once to total, count, average and find the largest.
activities.scenario: A table lists eight orders by region and product. A manager asks five questions; each answer is one formula in column G.
steps: G2: total revenue for the North (SUMIFS).
G3: units of Pen sold in the South (SUMIFS with two conditions).
G4: how many Book orders were for more than 3 units (COUNTIFS).
G5: average revenue of Pen orders (AVERAGEIFS).
G6: the largest North order by revenue (MAXIFS).

checks.label: G2 totals North revenue (470)
checks.explain: SUMIFS adds the cells in the first range for rows where every condition is true.

checks.label: G3 counts Pen units sold in the South (20)
checks.explain: Add a pair of range and condition for each extra condition.

checks.label: G4 counts Book orders over 3 units (2)
checks.explain: COUNTIFS has no range to add; it just counts rows where every pair is true.

checks.label: G5 averages Pen revenue (122.5)
checks.explain: The Pen revenues are 100, 200, 70 and 120.

checks.label: G6 finds the largest North order (250)
checks.explain: MAXIFS looks only at rows that meet the condition.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: Every range in one formula must be the same size.
checks.explain: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS give #VALUE! when the ranges differ in size.

activities.title: Find the top three
activities.objective: Rank values and pull out the names that go with the biggest ones.
activities.scenario: Seven students sat a test. Rank the first three, find the three highest scores, and name the students who earned them.
steps: In C2 rank Asha's score among all seven with RANK, locking the range. Fill C3 and C4.
In E2 find the highest score with LARGE; use 2 and 3 for E3 and E4.
In F2 find the name that goes with the score in E2: INDEX and MATCH. Fill F3 and F4.

checks.label: C2 ranks Asha 5th
checks.explain: RANK counts how many scores are higher and adds one. Lock the range so it does not slide.

checks.label: C3 ranks Bilal 1st
checks.explain: 91 is the highest of the seven.

checks.label: E2 is the highest score (91)
checks.explain: LARGE(range, k) gives the k-th largest value.

checks.label: E4 is the third highest score (85)
checks.explain: The order is 91, 88, 85.

checks.label: F2 names the top student (Bilal)
checks.explain: MATCH finds where the score sits, INDEX returns the name in that position.

checks.label: F4 names the third student (Chitra)
checks.explain: 85 belongs to Chitra.

activities.title: Weighted scores and shares of a total
activities.objective: Use SUMPRODUCT for a weighted result and a locked total for a share.
activities.scenario: A final grade is weighted by subject, and a shop wants each product's share of all the units it sold.
steps: In B6 work out the weighted grade: SUMPRODUCT of the weights and the scores.
In C9 work out Pen's share: its units divided by the total of B9:B11, with the total locked using dollar signs.
Do the same in C10 and C11, then format C9 as a percentage.

checks.label: B6 is the weighted grade (80)
checks.explain: SUMPRODUCT multiplies matching cells in two ranges and adds the results: 32 + 21 + 27.

checks.label: C9 is Pen's share (40%)
checks.explain: Lock the total with dollar signs so every row divides by the same number.

checks.label: C10 is Book's share (35%)
checks.explain: 35 out of 100 units.

checks.label: C11 is Bag's share (25%)
checks.explain: The three shares add to 100%.

checks.label: The shares in C9 are formatted as a percentage
checks.hint: Select C9 and choose Percent in the number format list.
checks.explain: A share reads better as 40% than 0.4.

activities.title: Clean a messy name list
activities.objective: Chain TRIM and PROPER to tidy names, then build an email address from the first name.
activities.scenario: Names were typed with stray spaces and mixed capitals. Clean them in column B, then build a lowercase email address in column C from the first name.
steps: In B2 clean A2: remove extra spaces with TRIM and fix the capitals with PROPER.
Fill B3 to B5.
In C2 take everything before the space in B2 (LEFT with FIND), make it lowercase, and join @example.org to it.
Fill C3 to C5.

checks.label: B2 is Asha Rao
checks.explain: TRIM removes extra spaces and PROPER capitalises each word. Functions can be nested, innermost first.

checks.label: B4 is Chitra Nair (the double space is gone)
checks.explain: TRIM keeps single spaces between words but removes the extras.

checks.label: C2 is asha@example.org
checks.explain: FIND gives the position of the space; LEFT takes the characters before it; & joins the text.

checks.label: C3 is bilal@example.org
checks.explain: The formula only works on the clean name, so build it from column B, not column A.

checks.label: C5 is dev@example.org
checks.explain: One formula, copied down, handles every row.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: If FIND shows #VALUE!, the name has no space in it.
checks.explain: FIND is case-sensitive and gives #VALUE! when it cannot find the text.

activities.title: Split product codes
activities.objective: Pull parts out of a code with LEFT, MID and RIGHT, turn them into numbers and rebuild a label with TEXT.
activities.scenario: Codes look like IN-2026-0042: country, year and serial number. Split each code into three columns, then rebuild an invoice label such as INV-0042.
steps: B2: the country (first two characters).
C2: the year as a number (MID then VALUE).
D2: the serial as a number (RIGHT then VALUE).
E2: a label that joins INV- to the serial padded to four digits with TEXT. Fill all three rows.

checks.label: B2 is IN
checks.explain: LEFT takes characters from the start.

checks.label: C2 is the number 2026
checks.explain: MID(text, start, length) takes from the middle; VALUE turns the text into a number you can calculate with.

checks.label: D2 is the number 42
checks.explain: RIGHT takes the last four characters, 0042, and VALUE makes it 42.

checks.label: E2 is INV-0042
checks.explain: TEXT with the format 0000 pads a number with leading zeros.

checks.label: C3 is 2025 (UK-2025-0107)
checks.explain: Each row has its own code.

checks.label: E4 is INV-0003
checks.hint: Same formulas on the last row.
checks.explain: 3 becomes 0003.

activities.title: A project schedule with dates
activities.objective: Do arithmetic with dates, count working days and format a result as a date.
activities.scenario: A project has three tasks, each with a start date and a number of days. Work out each due date, the working days between start and due, and the last day of the start month.
steps: In D2 add the days to the start date, then format D2 as a date.
Fill D3 and D4.
In E2 count the working days (Monday to Friday) from start to due with NETWORKDAYS.
In F2 find the last day of the start month with EOMONTH (use 0 months), formatted as a date.

checks.label: D2 is 12 March 2026
checks.explain: A date is a number of days, so adding days moves it forward.

checks.label: D3 is 8 April 2026
checks.explain: 9 March plus 30 days.

checks.label: D2 is formatted as a date
checks.hint: Select D2 and choose Date in the number format list.
checks.explain: A date without a date format shows as a plain number.

checks.label: E2 is 9 working days
checks.explain: NETWORKDAYS counts Monday to Friday, both ends included, so 2 March to 12 March is 9 days.

checks.label: F2 is 31 March 2026
checks.explain: EOMONTH with 0 gives the last day of the same month.

checks.label: F4 is 30 April 2026
checks.explain: April has 30 days.

activities.title: A pivot-style summary built with formulas
activities.objective: Build a region-by-product summary with one SUMIFS using mixed references, then total it and chart it.
activities.scenario: A PivotTable would summarise this data in seconds. Here you build the same summary by formula, so you can see exactly what a pivot does: one SUMIFS in every cell of a grid.
steps: In G2 write a SUMIFS for the region in F2 and the product in G1, using $ so one formula fits the whole grid.
Fill H2, G3:H5 the same way.
In I2 total the row, and fill I3 to I5.
Chart the region totals (F2:F5 as labels, I2:I5 as values) as a bar chart.

checks.label: G2 is North Pen revenue (220)
checks.explain: Lock the data ranges with $...$, lock the region column with $F2 and the product row with G$1, and one formula fits every cell.

spec.patternMsg: Use $F2 for the region and G$1 for the product, so the formula can be copied across and down.

checks.label: H2 is North Book revenue (250)
checks.explain: The product reference moves to H$1.

checks.label: G3 is South Pen revenue (200)
checks.explain: The region reference moves to $F3.

checks.label: H5 is West Book revenue (150)
checks.hint: Same formula in the last cell of the grid.
checks.explain: West sold only Book.

checks.label: G5 is West Pen revenue (0)
checks.explain: SUMIFS gives 0 when nothing matches, not an error.

checks.label: A bar chart of the region totals
checks.hint: Select F2:F5 as labels and I2:I5 as values, then add a bar chart.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares categories, which is exactly what regional totals are.

activities.title: Spot a trend and forecast
activities.objective: Use SLOPE and INTERCEPT to fit a straight line, forecast the next month and check how well the line fits with CORREL.
activities.scenario: Sales for six months are in B2:B7. Fit a straight line through them, use it to forecast month 7, and measure how closely the points follow a line.
steps: In E2 find the slope of sales against month (SLOPE with the sales range first).
In E3 find the intercept (INTERCEPT, same ranges).
In E4 forecast month 7: intercept plus slope times 7.
In E5 find the correlation between month and sales.

checks.label: E2 is the slope (about 9.74)
checks.explain: SLOPE takes the known y values (sales) first and the x values (months) second. It is how much sales rise per month.

checks.label: E3 is the intercept (91.4)
checks.explain: The intercept is where the line crosses zero months.

checks.label: E4 forecasts month 7 (about 159.6)
checks.explain: A straight line is intercept plus slope times x.

checks.label: E5 is the correlation (close to 1)
checks.explain: CORREL near 1 means the points sit very close to an upward line.

activities.title: Price a loan
activities.objective: Use PMT, and then check it by working out total interest and by finding how long a different payment would take.
activities.scenario: A laptop loan is 60,000 at 12% a year for 12 months. Find the monthly payment, the total paid and the interest cost; then find how many months a payment of 6,000 a month would take.
steps: In B4 find the monthly rate (the yearly rate divided by 12).
In B5 find the monthly payment with PMT, using the monthly rate, the number of months and the loan amount.
In B6 work out the total paid over the term (the payment times the months, shown as a positive number).
In B7 find the interest cost: total paid minus the loan.
In B8 find how many months a payment of 6,000 would take with NPER.

checks.label: B4 is the monthly rate (1%)
checks.explain: Divide the yearly rate by 12 to match monthly payments.

checks.label: B5 is the monthly payment (about -5,330.93)
checks.explain: PMT returns a negative number because it is money you pay out.

checks.label: B6 is the total paid (about 63,971.13)
checks.explain: The minus sign turns the payment into a positive amount.

checks.label: B7 is the interest cost (about 3,971.13)
checks.explain: You repay more than you borrowed; the difference is the interest.

checks.label: B8 is the months needed at 6,000 (about 10.6)
checks.explain: A bigger payment finishes the loan sooner.

activities.title: Is the project worth it? NPV and IRR
activities.objective: Compare an investment with a required return using NPV and IRR.
activities.scenario: A bakery can buy an oven for 100,000 today and expects extra cash of 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 over three years. The owner needs a 10% return. Is it worth it?
steps: In B7 find the net present value: NPV of the three years' cash at the discount rate, plus the investment (which is negative).
In B8 find the internal rate of return of all four cash flows with IRR.
In B9 decide: show Invest if the NPV is above zero, Skip if it is not.

checks.label: B7 is the NPV (about 22,765)
checks.explain: NPV discounts the cash from year 1 onwards, so add the year 0 amount outside it.

checks.label: B8 is the IRR (about 21.6%)
checks.explain: IRR is the discount rate that makes the NPV exactly zero.

checks.label: B9 says Invest
checks.explain: A positive NPV means the project beats the required return.

activities.title: Regional performance dashboard
activities.objective: Combine SUMIFS, division, nested decisions, RANK, INDEX with MATCH and a chart into one working dashboard.
activities.scenario: Three months of revenue by region sit in H1:J13. Targets for each region are in B2:B5. Build the dashboard: actual revenue, percent of target, a status, a rank, the best region by name, the company total and a chart.
steps: C2:C5: actual revenue per region with SUMIFS on the raw data (lock the data ranges).
D2:D5: percent of target (actual divided by target), formatted as a percentage in D2.
E2:E5: status with IF: On target at 100% or more, Close at 90% or more, otherwise Behind.
F2:F5: rank of each percent with RANK, locking the range.
B7: the best region by name (INDEX and MATCH on the biggest percent). B8: the company total.
Add a bar chart of actual revenue by region (A2:A5 as labels, C2:C5 as values).

checks.label: C2: North actual (530,000)
checks.explain: SUMIFS adds the revenue rows whose region matches the name in column A.

checks.label: D2: North is 106% of target
checks.explain: Percent of target is actual divided by target.

checks.label: D2 is formatted as a percentage
checks.explain: Show a ratio as a percentage so a reader sees 106%, not 1.06.

checks.label: E2: North is On target
checks.explain: Nest a second IF in the false part to add a middle band.

checks.label: E3: South is Close
checks.explain: 95% is below 100% but at least 90%.

checks.label: F2: North ranks 1st
checks.explain: North's 106% is the highest percentage.

checks.label: F3: South ranks 4th
checks.explain: South's 95% is the lowest.

checks.label: B7 names the best region (North)
checks.explain: Find the biggest percent, find its position, return the name in that position.

checks.label: A bar chart of actual revenue by region
checks.hint: Select A2:A5 as labels and C2:C5 as values.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares the regions at a glance.

checks.label: No error messages anywhere
checks.explain: A dashboard with a visible error loses trust at once.
